sections.brief: Open the stage where Stage Two stops: one sentence on the 26 July 1956 nationalization (Hahn: after the US and Britain refused aid; Eden's 'thumb on our windpipe'; Nasser's offer of compensation) with a link back to Stage Two, then the road to war in order: the London conferences and Dulles's 18-nation SCUA (9 September), Britain's hints of force, and the parallel crises FRUS names (violence on the Israel–Jordan border, the Iraqi proposal to move troops into Jordan, Israeli mobilization). Give Israel's case at full strength in its own words: Ben-Gurion's 15 October Knesset statement (242 casualties caused by Egypt in 1954–55; Egypt 'still sits in the Gaza Strip'), the Jewish Agency's 1,300 killed or wounded in 1948–56 and the Tiran closure of September 1955 (attributed as the Agency's figures), the Czech arms and the joint Egypt–Jordan–Syria command; link the Canal blockade to cw1's Resolution 95 section in one sentence. Then the dispute from both sides: Article 51 self-defence against the Katif Center's record that Gaza was listed as a war aim (and Ben-Gurion's rejected March 1955 proposal to retake it). Figure: timeline 26 July–28 October 1956; key figures (242; 1,300; 18 nations).

The collusion from the record, 14–25 October 1956: Challe and Gazier at Chequers on 14 October and Eden's 'So that lets us off the hook'; the Sèvres villa, 22–24 October, with every participant named; Dayan's Mitla 'real act of war' as pretext; the seven articles paraphrased one by one (render them as a comparison table: what each party committed); Ben-Gurion's 'fantastic' regional plan and the annexation point that never made the text; his demand for a written protocol against 'Perfidious Albion'; the signatures (Dean ad referendum, Pineau, Ben-Gurion), Eden's order to destroy every copy, and how the Israeli copy surfaced (BBC, 1996; Pineau's widow's pages, 2002). Tell the reactor promise of 24 October (and the 21 September agreement) in one paragraph and link forward to [scene:s11b|Dimona] and Stage Four. Present the dispute over motives from both sides (Shlaim's verdict, labelled as interpretation, against Israel's self-defence case and Oren). State plainly that Washington was not told (Hahn) and that Eden denied collusion for life. Figure: comparison of the seven articles; power structure of who met whom at Sèvres.

Kafr Qasim, 29 October 1956 only: the regime itself is Volume II's (link [scene:mg_s01|military government, 1949–66] via rd6_military_government in one sentence and do not retell it). In order: the curfew moved to 5 p.m. on the Triangle villages, the warning to the mukhtar at 4:30 p.m. (and the 3:30 p.m. order to the Border Police), the chain of command (Shadmi, Malinki, Dahan) with Malinki's testimony and Shadmi's denial both given, the some 400 villagers still in the fields, the nine shootings between 5 and 6:30 p.m., and the other villages where commanders did not shoot. Give every count with its source (47, 48, 49, 'fifty') and explain the unborn child; give 19 men, 6 women, 23 children and the 13 wounded. Then the silence: censorship, the 1 November internal inquiry, Toubi and Vilner's entry, Ben-Gurion's 12 November statement, the two-month blackout. Figure: process flow of the order (curfew decision → Shadmi → Malinki → Dahan's platoon → the village entrance); key figures. Answer the reader's question 'was this ordered from above?' only as far as this entry goes, and point to cw3_kafr_qasim_memory for Plan Mole.

The war itself, 29 October–22 December 1956. From egi_src_s02 and me_s08 tell only the Suez 1956 part (link back to rd6 for their earlier years and forward to cw4 for Iraq 1958). Israeli campaign first (17:00 on 29 October, the Mitla drop, Abu Ageila and Mitla resistance per the Library of Congress, Gaza on 2 November, Sharm el-Sheikh on 5 November, 100 hours), then Musketeer from Keightley's despatch (bombing from 31 October, Port Said and Port Fuad on 5–6 November, the 23:59 GMT cease-fire, 22,000 troops ashore at the peak, the 22 December evacuation). Then every casualty figure with its source and range, as a comparison table: Israel 150/170/171/172/189; Egypt about 1,030 to about 1,650 killed and 5,580 POWs exchanged on 27 December; Port Said 650 plus 100 at Port Fuad (a British estimate, civilian share unclear); Britain 16 or 21 killed; France 10. Present the dispute over whether Egypt was beaten or withdrew (Nasser's claim vs the IDF). Close with Ben-Gurion's 'war deluxe' warning of 27 December. Map: me_layers (the coup-decade node); figure: timeline 29 October–22 December; key figures.

Washington against its allies, 30 October–22 December 1956, now from the primary UN record: the Anglo-French vetoes of the US and Soviet drafts (30 October); Resolution 119 (31 October, 7–2, France and Britain against, Australia and Belgium abstaining) calling the first emergency special session; Resolution 997 (US draft, adopted about 4:20 a.m. on 2 November, 64–5–6, with the five noes and six abstainers named and Pearson's reason for abstaining); 998 and 1000 (57–0–19 each, the UNEF resolutions) and 999 (59–5–12); 1002 of 7 November (65–1–10) calling 'once again' for withdrawal. Then the money and oil levers: the reserve drain below the $2 billion floor, Humphrey's condition ('conforming to rather than defying the United Nations'), the $561 million IMF drawing and $739 million stand-by of December, and the Middle East Emergency Committee oil plan held back until withdrawal ('we have held up this measure', 25 November). Close with UNEF's arrival on 15 November, the 22 December exit and the US–UK repair. Still open: the operative texts of 998, 999, 1000 and 1001 were not fetched; describe them only as the UNEF resolutions. Present the dispute over whether money or principle decided it, from both sides. Figures: comparison table of the GA votes (resolution, date, yes–no–abstain, who voted no); money chain (offensive → reserve drain → US condition → IMF package → withdrawal).

Khan Yunis (3 November) and Rafah (12 November) 1956, built on the UNRWA Director's special report (A/3212/Add.1), quoted by paragraph: 275 listed at Khan Yunis (140 refugees, 135 residents), 111 at Rafah (103 refugees, 7 residents, 1 Egyptian), 66 more (48 refugees) in smaller incidents 1–21 November, and the Director's stated limits (UNTSO blocked, deaths unverifiable, lists never complete). Give both accounts exactly as the report does (Israeli: resistance and hostility; refugees: resistance had ended, unarmed civilians killed) and the Director's own Rafah finding (unheard loudspeakers, panicked soldiers). Then every other figure with its source: Israel's 48 for Rafah; Palestinian 415 (+57 missing) and 197 (+23); Rantisi's 525; Sacco's witnesses; The Times's 'some 60'; Morris's 'about two hundred' and his use of the word massacre. Set the fedayeen raids from Gaza beside it as Israel's context, without letting context answer the question of what happened. Figure: comparison table of figures by source; key figures. Answer the reader's 'was anyone held to account?' plainly: the sources found record no Israeli investigation.

Moscow and Budapest, 4–17 November 1956: the Soviet crushing of Hungary the same week (US condemnation; Eisenhower to King Saud on 16 November), and the Soviet notes of 5 November, now from their texts: to Ben-Gurion ('playing with the fate of peace ... in a criminal and irresponsible manner'; a question mark 'upon the very existence of Israel as a State'; the ambassador recalled), to Mollet ('all modern forms of destructive weaponry', CVCE summary), and JTA's 23 November report of the common demands (withdrawal, reparations to Egypt, UN force on both sides of the lines). Ben-Gurion's replies of 8 November ('not and will not be decided by any foreign factor') and 17 November ('a return to murder, blockade, and boycott'). Present the dispute over what ended the war (the Soviet threat vs American pressure) from both sides. Link to [scene:cia_s03|the Khrushchev speech] in one sentence. Still open: the Bulganin letter to Eden was not fetched. Figure: timeline 23 October–17 November 1956 with Hungary and Suez on parallel rows.

Victory and retreat in about 36 hours, 6–8 November 1956: Ben-Gurion's letter read by Dayan at Sharm el-Sheikh (Yotvat 'will return to be part of the Third Kingdom of Israel', from Walla's Hebrew quotation, and Avnery's recollection labelled as an opponent's memory); the 7 November Knesset speech's seven points ('dead and buried', no foreign force on Israeli-held ground, peace talks without preconditions); Eisenhower's message of 7 November with its delivery times and its warning; Ben-Gurion's 8 November reply ('never planned to annex the Sinai desert'); the government's 8 November statement and its three aims. Add Eban–Rountree on 8 November, Begin's 16 November position, and Bar-Joseph's note that the 1956 memory shaped June 1967. Present the dispute over what the 'Third Kingdom' language meant from both sides. Figure: comparison of the 7 November speech and the 8 November reply, line by line.

The Jews of Egypt, November 1956–1958, picking up from Volume II's rd6_exodus (one sentence linking back): the arrests (about 1,000 detained; about 900 by 7 November; the Abbasiya and Les Barrages camps), the expulsion waves, Nationality Law No. 391 of 22 November 1956 and its undefined 'Zionist' clause, the 23 November proclamation that 'all Jews are Zionists and enemies of the state', sequestration under Military Proclamation No. 4 (486 persons and firms listed, at least 95% Jewish; about 500 companies by March 1957), the 'ONE WAY-NO RETURN' exit visas and property 'donations', and the 23,000–25,000 who left by 1957–58 (community about 15,000 by 1957). Name the antisemitism of the proclamation and the law plainly as state acts; never generalize about Egyptians or Muslims; give the limits Julius herself records (Egyptian-national Jews initially spared, some orders rescinded) and present the dispute over causes from both sides (Julius and Krämer vs Beinin, with Mendes from rd6). Attribute carefully: the legal details come from an advocacy report (JJAC) and an advocacy author (Julius); the numbers are corroborated by JTA. Still open: the texts of Law 391 and Proclamation No. 4 themselves, and the number of British and French nationals expelled. Link [scene:s00e3|the two displacements] in one sentence. Figure: key figures (1,000; 486; 95%; 23,000–25,000); timeline 29 October 1956–1958.

Israel's first occupation of Gaza, November 1956–8 March 1957: the military government over some 300,000 people (three-quarters refugees), the curfew and screening as UNRWA describes them, UNRWA's warning, the councils, schools and textbooks, police stations, the Bedouin removal order (Nelson, 16 December), and the destroyed Hafiz monuments. Then the plan to keep it: Ben-Gurion on 19 December and 23 January ('This Strip was never Egyptian'), the 13 January cabinet resolution, the Knesset vote of 23 January, the 'Blueprint for Gaza', the Nahal outpost at Rafiah. Present the dispute (retention vs security-only) from both sides. Figure: power structure of Gaza under Israeli rule (military governor, councils, local police under Israel Police, UNRWA alongside); timeline November 1956–March 1957.

The withdrawal fight, January–8 March 1957, from the primary record: Resolutions 1123 (19 January) and 1124 (2 February, 74–2–2, 'Deplores the non-compliance'); the 11 February aide-mémoire from its text (Gaza withdrawal 'prompt and unconditional'; UNEF on the Gaza boundary; the Gulf as 'international waters'; the US 'prepared to exercise the right of free and innocent passage'); Eban's reading of it the same day; the FRUS embassy reports of 15, 18–19 and 22 February ('fight or submit'; 'double standard of morality'; 'every ounce of our moral strength'); the 20 February bipartisan meeting (Dulles naming reparations, bonds and US aid as levers; Knowland's 30-day sanctions text; Johnson, Fulbright and Rayburn's resistance) and Dulles's letter to Johnson; Eisenhower's 20 February address quoted directly ('impose conditions on its own withdrawal?'; 'no choice but to exert pressure'); Dulles on 28 February ('unconditional withdrawal' with stated 'assumptions'); Meir's 1 March statement; the withdrawal from Gaza on 8 March. Embed aid_arms:Leverage & Law:1 and say what it leaves out (its first case is 1987, the Lavi at about $1.8B; then the $10B guarantees held 120 days in 1991–92), and aid_arms:Overview:2 ('Economic aid and loans only', 1948–1961) to show what was at stake beside the bonds and reparations Dulles named. Present the sanctions dispute and the guarantees dispute from both sides. Still open: Eisenhower's 2 March letter to Ben-Gurion was not fetched (known only through Ben-Gurion's 5 March account). Link forward to [scene:s12|May–June 1967] and [scene:iaa_s04|1967]. Figure: comparison of what Israel asked for and what the aide-mémoire and address gave.

The trial and what followed, 1957–1960: the military court under Benjamin Halevy (case MD/57/3), the sessions from March 1957, the verdict of 16 October 1958 with every name and sentence (17, 15, 15 and five of 7 years), the court's words on unlawful orders and Halevy's black-flag test, the reactions (families, Laskov, Herut, the village elders, Falastin), Shadmi's separate trial and the competing descriptions of his fine (10 prutot = one hundredth of a lira; show the JVL and PalQuest discrepancies), the reductions step by step and the releases by late 1959, and Malinki's and Dahan's later posts. Present the accountability dispute from both sides, with Orbach's reading of how the doctrine was made and Leibowitz's protest. Figure: timeline of the sentences from verdict to release; comparison of sentence imposed vs time served.

After the trial: compensation (IL5,000 per victim plus IL1,000 for the pregnant woman; IL500,000 in all per the Encyclopaedia Judaica; Issa's 700 lira), the state-organized sulha of 20 November 1957 and Robinson's and Slyomovics's readings of it, the 1976 monument, the 2006 museum, then the long argument over Plan Mole: Segev's 'contingency plan to expel', the 2017–2022 legal fight for the records (dates), Levy's testimony on Shadmi's 'desirable' fatalities, and the fact that the plan's text stays redacted. Present the expulsion-plan dispute from both sides as the entry does. End with Peres (2007), Rivlin (2014) and Herzog (2021) in their exact words and the Knesset's rejection of the recognition bill (93–12, 26 October 2021). This section runs past 1957; say so and keep the post-1966 material to the documented memory record. Figure: timeline 1957–2022.

Closing synthesis: the architecture as it stood in spring 1957. Eden's fall and the US–UK repair under Macmillan; the Eisenhower Doctrine from its text: the 5 January request, the House vote of 30 January (355–61) and the Senate's of 5 March (72–19), Public Law 85-7 of 9 March section by section (economic aid; armed force against aggression 'from any country controlled by international communism'; up to $200 million from existing Mutual Security funds, no new appropriation; support for UNEF; reports twice a year), Russell's 'small war' warning, and Hahn's list of recipients (Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Libya; not Israel). Present the Doctrine dispute (communism by its text vs replacing Britain and France) and 'who won' from both sides (Oren against Shlaim and Fromkin as Oren reports them; Hahn on Nasser). Israel's gains (Tiran, UNEF, the French alliance and reactor) and costs; the Trident and periphery story linked forward to [scene:ira_s00c|the periphery] and Stage Four. Close with Ben-Gurion's warning that the next war might be long and fought without foreign help. Still open: the Richards mission's allocations. Figures: synthesis power-structure diagram of spring 1957; money chain for the Doctrine (Congress → up to $200M of existing funds → named states → stated aim, containment → who was left out).
